learningObjectives.title: Periods, groups, blocks, and where metals and non-metals sit
Reading electron configuration from position, and the named families
Explaining the trends: radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity
Group 1 and group 17: trends in reactivity and the reactions that show them
Oxides from basic to acidic, acid rain and ocean acidification

questions.q: Which element is classified as a metalloid?
options: Silicon
Aluminium
Iodine
Scandium
optionWhy: Silicon lies on the stepped line between metals and non-metals and has intermediate properties: it is a shiny solid but a semiconductor, and its oxide is acidic. The metalloids are boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium.

A student who counts every element touching the stepped line as a metalloid picks aluminium. Aluminium borders the line on the metal side and is a typical metal: shiny, malleable and a good electrical conductor.
A student who classifies by appearance picks iodine because its crystals are shiny. Iodine is a non-metal in group 17: a molecular solid of I₂ that does not conduct electricity.

A student who reads 'transition' as 'between metal and non-metal' picks this d-block element. Scandium, like every transition element, is a metal; the metalloids are in the p-block along the stepped line.
questions.explain: Silicon lies on the stepped line between metals and non-metals and has intermediate properties: it is a shiny solid but a semiconductor, and its oxide is acidic. The metalloids are boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium.

questions.q: Selenium is in period 4 and group 16 of the periodic table. Which statement about a selenium atom is correct?
options: It has sixteen valence electrons, in the fourth energy level
It has four valence electrons, located in the sixth energy level
It has six valence electrons, in the fourth energy level
It has only two valence electrons, in the fourth energy level
optionWhy: A student who takes the group number (1–18) as the number of valence electrons gets sixteen. With the 1–18 numbering, a p-block atom has (group number − 10) valence electrons, so selenium has six.

A student who swaps the roles of period and group takes the period (4) as the number of valence electrons and reads group 16 as the old group VI, placing them in the sixth level. The period number (4) gives the outer energy level, and the group gives the valence electrons (16 − 10 = 6).
Period 4 means the outer electrons are in the fourth energy level; group 16 means 16 − 10 = 6 valence electrons. The configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴, with 4s² 4p⁴ in the outer level.
A student who confuses valence electrons with valency counts the two electrons selenium needs to reach eight. Selenium has six valence electrons (4s² 4p⁴); its valency of 2 is a separate idea.
questions.explain: Period 4 means the outer electrons are in the fourth energy level; group 16 means 16 − 10 = 6 valence electrons. The configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴, with 4s² 4p⁴ in the outer level.

options: Krypton
Iodine
Manganese
Hydrogen
optionWhy: A student who merges the two right-hand groups picks krypton. Krypton is a noble gas in group 18, with a full outer level; the halogens are the adjacent group 17.
The halogens are the group 17 elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. Iodine atoms have seven valence electrons (5s² 5p⁵) and the element exists as I₂ molecules.

A student who carries over the old 'group VII' label into the 1–18 numbering looks in group 7 and finds manganese. Group 7 is a d-block group; the halogens, with seven valence electrons, are group 17.
A student who groups hydrogen with the halogens, because it forms H₂ and H⁻ as they form X₂ and X⁻, picks hydrogen. Hydrogen is not in group 17; the halogens are fluorine to astatine.
questions.explain: The halogens are the group 17 elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. Iodine atoms have seven valence electrons (5s² 5p⁵) and the element exists as I₂ molecules.

questions.q: How, and why, does atomic radius change across period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
options: It increases, as each atom has more electrons, which need more space
It increases, as the nucleus's attraction is shared out among more electrons
It decreases, as nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same level
It decreases, as atoms closer to a full outer shell are more stable and compact
optionWhy: A student who thinks more electrons means a bigger atom picks this. Atomic radius decreases across the period; the extra electrons enter the same energy level while the nuclear charge rises, so they are pulled in.

A student who pictures the nuclear attraction as a fixed amount shared out among the electrons picks this. The attraction on each electron depends on nuclear charge and distance and is not divided up; radius decreases across the period.

Across period 3 the nuclear charge increases from +11 to +17, while the added electrons go into the third energy level, where they shield each other very little. The outer electrons are pulled closer, so atomic radius decreases.

A student who uses the stability of a full shell as a cause picks this. The direction is right but the reason is not: size is explained by the increasing nuclear charge acting on electrons in the same energy level, not by a drive towards a full shell.
questions.explain: Across period 3 the nuclear charge increases from +11 to +17, while the added electrons go into the third energy level, where they shield each other very little. The outer electrons are pulled closer, so atomic radius decreases.

questions.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
options: Neon, Ne
Chlorine, Cl
Iodine, I
Fluorine, F
optionWhy: A student who extends the trend to the end of the period picks neon. Electronegativity refers to attracting a bonding pair, and neon forms no covalent bonds in ordinary conditions, so it is not given a Pauling value.

A student who treats electronegativity as electron affinity picks chlorine, which has the most negative first electron affinity (−349 kJ mol⁻¹). Electronegativity is a different property, and fluorine's is the highest.

A student who thinks more protons always means a stronger pull picks iodine. Down group 17 the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so electronegativity decreases; iodine is the least electronegative of these halogens.

Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so fluorine, at the top of group 17, is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale). Its small atoms attract a bonding pair strongly.
questions.explain: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so fluorine, at the top of group 17, is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale). Its small atoms attract a bonding pair strongly.

questions.q: A small piece of sodium is added to a large volume of water containing universal indicator. Which statement describes what happens?
options: Hydrogen and sodium oxide form, and the oxide stays as a solid
Hydrogen gas is released, so the solution turns acidic
Hydrogen and sodium hydroxide form, so the solution turns alkaline
The sodium dissolves unchanged, and the fizzing is air escaping
optionWhy: A student who expects the metal oxide as product picks this. Sodium reacts with cold water to form sodium hydroxide, which dissolves; even sodium oxide would react with water to give sodium hydroxide.
A student who links hydrogen with acids picks this. Hydrogen gas is not an acid; the reaction leaves hydroxide ions in solution, so the solution becomes alkaline.
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). The sodium fizzes as hydrogen is released, and the hydroxide ions formed turn the indicator to an alkaline colour.
A student who confuses reacting with dissolving picks this. Sodium reacts: the gas is hydrogen (it pops with a lighted splint), and the solution contains sodium hydroxide, not sodium metal.
questions.explain: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). The sodium fizzes as hydrogen is released, and the hydroxide ions formed turn the indicator to an alkaline colour.

questions.q: Bromine water is added separately to aqueous potassium chloride and to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation is expected?
options: A reaction occurs with the potassium chloride only
There is no reaction with either of the two solutions
A reaction occurs with both of the salt solutions
A reaction occurs with the potassium iodide only
optionWhy: A student who thinks reactivity increases down every group expects bromine to displace chlorine. Down group 17 oxidizing ability decreases, so bromine reacts with iodide but not chloride ions.
A student who thinks halide ions are unreactive because they have full outer shells picks this. Iodide ions are oxidized by bromine, which attracts electrons more strongly than iodine does.
A student who thinks all halogens behave identically expects bromine to react with both. A halogen oxidizes only the halide ions of halogens below it, so bromine reacts with iodide only.

Bromine oxidizes iodide ions, which are below it in group 17: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), and the solution darkens to brown. Bromine cannot oxidize chloride ions, because chlorine attracts electrons more strongly than bromine.
questions.explain: Bromine oxidizes iodide ions, which are below it in group 17: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), and the solution darkens to brown. Bromine cannot oxidize chloride ions, because chlorine attracts electrons more strongly than bromine.

questions.q: Which statement about ocean acidification is correct?
options: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH, but seawater stays alkaline
Seawater has now become acidic, with a pH below 7, because of absorbed CO₂
Acid rain falling on the sea is the main cause of the fall in seawater pH
Warmer seawater dissolves more CO₂, which is the main reason the pH is falling
optionWhy: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq), and carbonic acid releases H⁺ ions. The average surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times: seawater is less alkaline, not acidic.
A student who reads 'acidification' as 'becoming acidic' picks this. The pH is falling, but at about 8.1 seawater is still above 7.

A student who merges the two environmental problems picks this. The main cause is the absorption of atmospheric CO₂; acid rain from sulfur and nitrogen oxides has only a small effect on the whole ocean.
A student who assumes gases dissolve better when warm picks this. Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises; the pH falls because the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere has risen.
questions.explain: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq), and carbonic acid releases H⁺ ions. The average surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times: seawater is less alkaline, not acidic.

questions.q: Which statement about aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, is correct?
options: It reacts with acids only, as every metal oxide is basic
It reacts with bases only, as it is a p-block non-metal oxide
It reacts with neither acids nor bases, being neutral
It reacts with both acids and bases, since it is amphoteric
optionWhy: A student who has learned that every metal oxide is basic picks this. Aluminium oxide does react with acids, but it also reacts with bases such as sodium hydroxide: it is amphoteric, part of the continuum from basic to acidic oxides.
A student who thinks the p-block holds only non-metals treats aluminium oxide as a non-metal oxide, and so as acidic. Aluminium is a metal, and its oxide reacts with acids as well as with bases.

A student who reads 'amphoteric', between basic and acidic, as 'neutral' picks this. An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases; aluminium oxide's insolubility in water does not make it unreactive towards them.

Aluminium oxide is amphoteric: it reacts with acids, for example Al₂O₃(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l), and also with bases such as sodium hydroxide. In period 3 it lies between the basic oxides of sodium and magnesium and the acidic oxides of the non-metals.
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric: it reacts with acids, for example Al₂O₃(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l), and also with bases such as sodium hydroxide. In period 3 it lies between the basic oxides of sodium and magnesium and the acidic oxides of the non-metals.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in the nitrite ion?
optionWhy: A student who makes the oxidation states sum to zero gets x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4. In an ion they must sum to the ion's charge, −1, giving +3.
A student who treats the oxidation state as the actual charge on the ion gives nitrogen the ion's charge, −1. Oxidation states are assigned atom by atom; nitrogen in NO₂⁻ is +3.
A student who swaps the endings uses nitrate, NO₃⁻: x + 3(−2) = −1, so x = +5. Nitrite is NO₂⁻, with nitrogen +3; +5 is nitrogen in nitrate.
Nitrite is NO₂⁻. With oxygen −2 and the sum equal to the ion's charge: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3. This matches the rule that the '-ite' ion has the lower oxidation state.
questions.explain: Nitrite is NO₂⁻. With oxygen −2 and the sum equal to the ion's charge: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3. This matches the rule that the '-ite' ion has the lower oxidation state.
questions.working: The nitrite ion is NO₂⁻. Oxygen is −2 and the oxidation states sum to the charge on the ion: x + 2(−2) = −1, so x = +3.

questions.q: Every atom in an uncombined element, such as O₂ or Cl₂, has an oxidation state of zero. Why?
options: It has no overall charge, so each of its atoms must also be zero
Oxidation states are given only to ions, and it contains none
Its atoms are all identical, so no electrons are transferred between them
Its atoms already have full outer shells by sharing, so they need no transfer
optionWhy: A student who equates each atom's oxidation state with the overall charge picks this. Water is neutral, yet hydrogen is +1 and oxygen −2; elements are zero because their atoms are identical.
A student who thinks oxidation states are real ionic charges picks this. Oxidation states are assigned to atoms in covalent molecules too, such as carbon (+4) in CO₂.

An oxidation state shows the electrons transferred in forming a bond. Between identical atoms there is no difference in attraction for electrons, so no atom gains or loses electrons relative to another, and each is zero.

A student who explains chemistry by atoms reaching stable full shells picks this. Chlorine also has a full outer shell by sharing in HCl, yet there it is −1; the oxidation state of an element is zero because identical atoms do not transfer electrons to one another.
questions.explain: An oxidation state shows the electrons transferred in forming a bond. Between identical atoms there is no difference in attraction for electrons, so no atom gains or loses electrons relative to another, and each is zero.
